```{r setup}
results_dir <- Sys.getenv("KAPPA_JACK_BOUNDARY_RESULTS_DIR", unset = "results")
required <- file.path(results_dir, c("summary.csv", "diagnostics.csv", "metadata.csv"))
missing <- required[!file.exists(required)]
if (length(missing) > 0L) {
  stop(paste0(
    "Missing experiment results. Run `Rscript run_experiment.R ",
    "--reps 1000 --bootstrap-reps 399 --progress` first."
  ))
}
summary <- read.csv(required[[1L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
diagnostics <- read.csv(required[[2L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
metadata_raw <- read.csv(required[[3L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
metadata <- setNames(metadata_raw$value, metadata_raw$key)

fmt <- function(x, digits = 3L) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
method_order <- c(
  "wald_if_z", "wald_if_fisher", "jack_t", "jack_fisher_delta_t",
  "jack_fisher_direct_t", "jack_fisher_direct_boundary", "bca",
  "bca_boundary", "bootstrap_t_jack", "bootstrap_t_jack_boundary"
)
summary <- summary[order(summary$n, match(summary$method, method_order)), ]
cell <- function(method, n, column) {
  summary[summary$method == method & summary$n == n, column][[1L]]
}
```

## Question

Can delete-one jackknife variance estimation and a boundary-aware calibration
repair the poor small-sample coverage found in Experiment 47?

The data-generating problem is deliberately unchanged: five exchangeable
raters, five uniformly distributed ordered categories, true quadratic Fleiss
kappa `r fmt(as.numeric(metadata[["target"]]), 2)`, complete data, and
$n\in\{20,30\}$. Holding the problem fixed isolates the interval machinery.

## Short Answer

```{r short-answer}
n_grid <- sort(unique(summary$n))
direct_candidate <- "jack_fisher_direct_boundary"
direct_text <- paste(vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  sprintf(
    "n = %d: coverage %s, mean length %s, fallback %s",
    n, fmt(cell(direct_candidate, n, "coverage")),
    fmt(cell(direct_candidate, n, "mean_length")),
    fmt(cell(direct_candidate, n, "fallback_rate"))
  )
}, character(1)), collapse = "; ")
bootstrap_text <- paste(vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  sprintf(
    "n = %d: coverage %s, mean length %s",
    n, fmt(cell("bootstrap_t_jack_boundary", n, "coverage")),
    fmt(cell("bootstrap_t_jack_boundary", n, "mean_length"))
  )
}, character(1)), collapse = "; ")
variance_text <- paste(vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  sprintf(
    "n = %d: IF %s, jackknife %s",
    n, fmt(cell("wald_if_z", n, "if_se_ratio")),
    fmt(cell("wald_if_z", n, "jackknife_se_ratio"))
  )
}, character(1)), collapse = "; ")
boundary_text <- paste(vapply(n_grid, function(n) {
  d <- diagnostics[diagnostics$n == n, ]
  sprintf(
    "n = %d: exact %s, leave-one-out %s",
    n, fmt(d$exact_agreement_rate), fmt(d$leave_one_out_boundary_rate)
  )
}, character(1)), collapse = "; ")
best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(summary, summary$n), function(d) {
  d <- d[d$failures == 0L, ]
  d[which.min(abs(d$coverage - 0.95)), ]
}))
best_text <- paste(sprintf(
  "n = %d: %s at %s", best$n, best$method_label, fmt(best$coverage)
), collapse = "; ")
```

The raw-scale delete-one jackknife is not enough. It raises the estimated
standard error, but only modestly: mean SE / empirical SD is `r variance_text`.
The useful change is **transformed studentization plus an explicit boundary
rule**. Direct Fisher-scale jackknife-t with that rule gives `r direct_text`.
The more expensive jackknife-studentized bootstrap gives `r bootstrap_text`;
it is longer and slightly conservative at $n=30$, so it has no clear payoff
in this cell. The closest rows to nominal coverage are `r best_text`.

The boundary is not just the event $\hat\kappa=1$. A leave-one-out sample can
hit one even when the original sample does not: `r boundary_text`. That is why
the direct transformed jackknife and the studentized bootstrap need a defined
fallback for sparse-disagreement samples. The result is promising enough for a
larger grid, but this one-cell experiment does not establish a generally valid
small-sample interval.

## Evidence

```{r evidence-table}
tab <- data.frame(
  `n` = summary$n,
  Method = summary$method_label,
  Coverage = fmt(summary$coverage),
  `Valid-Only Coverage` = fmt(summary$coverage_valid),
  `MC SE` = fmt(summary$coverage_mcse),
  `Miss Below` = fmt(summary$miss_below),
  `Miss Above` = fmt(summary$miss_above),
  `Mean Length` = fmt(summary$mean_length),
  `Fallback Rate` = fmt(summary$fallback_rate),
  Failures = summary$failures,
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(tab, align = "rlrrrrrrrr")
```

Coverage counts an unavailable interval as a miss. “Boundary” methods are
hybrids: they use the named interior interval whenever it exists and substitute
the one-sided boundary interval only when the interior calculation degenerates.
All reported intervals are intersected with the quadratic Fleiss parameter
space $[-1/(R-1),1]$; this changes length, not coverage for an interior truth.

```{r calibration-table}
cal <- unique(summary[, c(
  "n", "bias", "empirical_sd", "mean_if_se", "mean_jackknife_se",
  "if_se_ratio", "jackknife_se_ratio"
)])
cal <- cal[order(cal$n), ]
cal_tab <- data.frame(
  `n` = cal$n,
  Bias = fmt(cal$bias, 4),
  `Empirical SD` = fmt(cal$empirical_sd, 4),
  `Mean IF SE` = fmt(cal$mean_if_se, 4),
  `Mean Jackknife SE` = fmt(cal$mean_jackknife_se, 4),
  `IF SE / SD` = fmt(cal$if_se_ratio),
  `Jackknife SE / SD` = fmt(cal$jackknife_se_ratio),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cal_tab, align = "rrrrrrr")
```

```{r boundary-table}
boundary_tab <- data.frame(
```

## Mathematical construction

### Quadratic Fleiss functional

For subject $i$, define


$$
 m_i=R^{-1}\sum_jY_{ij},\qquad
 q_i=R^{-1}\sum_jY_{ij}^2,\qquad
 d_i={\binom R2}^{-1}\sum_{j<k}(Y_{ij}-Y_{ik})^2.
$$

Writing bars for subject averages, the complete-data quadratic Fleiss
coefficient is the smooth three-moment functional

$$
 \hat\kappa=1-\frac{\bar d}{2(\bar q-\bar m^2)}.
$$

The IF rows use the delta covariance returned by
`kappa_counts(estimator = "fleiss_cuzick", weight = "quadratic")`. The runner
independently reconstructs the same point estimate and IF standard error from
these three moments and records their maximum numerical discrepancies.

### Delete-one jackknife

Let $\hat\kappa_{(-i)}$ denote the same functional after deleting subject $i$,
and let $\bar\kappa_{(-\cdot)}=n^{-1}\sum_i\hat\kappa_{(-i)}$. The jackknife
variance estimate is

$$
 \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{J}(\hat\kappa)
 =\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
   \{\hat\kappa_{(-i)}-\bar\kappa_{(-\cdot)}\}^2.
$$

`Jackknife SE, t` inserts its square root in a $t_{n-1}$ interval. The delta
Fisher row transforms $\hat\kappa$ with
$g(\kappa)=\operatorname{atanh}(\kappa)$ and uses
$g'(\hat\kappa)\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_J$. The direct Fisher row instead
jackknifes $g(\hat\kappa_{(-i)})$ itself. That distinction matters near one,
where the linear delta approximation is poor, but the direct calculation is
undefined as soon as an original or leave-one-out estimate equals one.

### BCa and jackknife-studentized bootstrap

Each outer bootstrap sample resamples whole subjects. BCa uses the empirical
bias correction

$$
 z_0=\Phi^{-1}\!\left\{
   \Pr_*(\hat\kappa^*<\hat\kappa)
   +\tfrac12\Pr_*(\hat\kappa^*=\hat\kappa)
 \right\}
$$

and jackknife acceleration

$$
 a=\frac{\sum_i(\bar\kappa_{(-\cdot)}-\hat\kappa_{(-i)})^3}
 {6[\sum_i(\bar\kappa_{(-\cdot)}-\hat\kappa_{(-i)})^2]^{3/2}}.
$$

The studentized bootstrap recomputes a delete-one jackknife standard error
inside every bootstrap sample,

$$
 T_b^*=\frac{\hat\kappa_b^*-\hat\kappa}
                {\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_{J,b}^*},
 \qquad
 C_{t}=
 \left[\hat\kappa-q^*_{.975}\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_J,
       \hat\kappa-q^*_{.025}\widehat{\mathrm{se}}_J\right].
$$

At least 70% of the requested $T_b^*$ values must be finite. This method is
more expensive than BCa because every outer draw contains an inner jackknife,
but the three-moment formula makes it practical here.

### Exact-agreement fallback

Let $D_i=d_i/(y_{\max}-y_{\min})^2\in[0,1]$,
$A=E(D_i)$, and $B$ be chance disagreement on the same normalized scale.
Then

$$
 \kappa=1-A/B,\qquad A\leq p:=\Pr(D_i>0).
$$

If $K=\sum_i1(D_i>0)$, the fallback uses the one-sided Clopper--Pearson
upper limit

$$
 p_U=F^{-1}_{\mathrm{Beta}(K+1,n-K)}(1-\alpha/2)
$$

when $K<n$, and $p_U=1$ otherwise. It combines this with a one-sided
jackknife-t lower limit $B_L$ for chance disagreement and reports

$$
 C_{\partial}=\left[\max\{-1/(R-1),\;1-p_U/B_L\},\;1\right].
$$

The two component errors are allocated $\alpha/2$ each. The inequality
$A\le p$ makes the disagreement part conservative and valid without modeling
positive-event severity. Only the binomial component is exact: $B_L$ remains
a small-sample jackknife approximation, so $C_{\partial}$ is a principled
hybrid to test, not an exact finite-sample kappa interval.

## Sources and relation to prior work

The coefficient and its asymptotic IF variance follow
[Moss (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-023-09945-2). The simulation uses
the knowledge/guessing construction associated with
[Perreault and Leigh (1989)](https://doi.org/10.1177/002224378902600201); with
uniform guessing and knowledge probability $\sqrt{\kappa}$, the population
quadratic Fleiss coefficient is $\kappa$.

The delete-one variance formula is the classical jackknife construction; see
[Efron and Stein (1981)](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176345462). BCa is from
[Efron (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478410), and the BCa /
bootstrap-t accuracy rationale is summarized by
[DiCiccio and Efron (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1214/ss/1032280214). The exact
binomial limit is from
[Clopper and Pearson (1934)](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/26.4.404).

Ordinary empirical resampling is not automatically valid when an estimator can
land on a parameter boundary; [Andrews
(2000)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00114) gives a canonical bootstrap
inconsistency result. That theorem is not asserted directly for this kappa
functional. It is the reason to expose and measure the boundary mass instead of
assuming that BCa or bootstrap-t must repair it.

Archived Experiment 08 already compared ordinary percentile, basic, BCa, and
IF-studentized bootstrap intervals. The new ingredients here are the delete-one
standard error inside every bootstrap draw, direct transformed jackknifing, and
the explicit exact-agreement fallback. Archived Experiments 12--13 tried rare
count and hurdle intervals as defaults; this experiment uses the bounded-event
argument only when a smoother interior method fails.

## Caveats

- The first pass is one favorable-to-interpretation complete-data DGP. The
  extension broadens its margins and disagreement geometry, but still does not
  cover missingness, lower agreement, or arbitrary rater dependence.
- A boundary fallback can improve coverage by being wide. Mean length and
  fallback frequency therefore matter as much as aggregate coverage.
- Monte Carlo uncertainty is reported, but bootstrap quantiles also have inner
  simulation error from `r metadata[["bootstrap_reps"]]` draws.
- The boundary interval is only partly exact. A final method would need theory
  for the chance-disagreement lower limit or a direct test inversion for the
  full ratio functional.

```sh
Rscript experiments/workbench/48-small-n-jackknife-boundary/run_experiment.R --smoke --progress
```

Focused run used here (single-core by design):

```sh
Rscript experiments/workbench/48-small-n-jackknife-boundary/run_experiment.R \
  --reps 1000 --bootstrap-reps 399 --cores 1 --progress
```

The run used seed base `r metadata[["seed_base"]]`,
`r metadata[["reps"]]` Monte Carlo replications per cell, and completed in
`r fmt(as.numeric(metadata[["elapsed_seconds"]]), 1)` seconds. Raw replicate
rows are local-only; the committed summary, diagnostics, and metadata are the
reproducibility record.

## Extension: same kappa, different disagreement geometry

The first pass used only one DGP: the Perreault--Leigh (PL)
knowledge/guessing construction with uniform category probabilities,
exchangeable raters, and conditionally independent rating errors. This
extension keeps five raters, five categories, true quadratic Fleiss kappa
0.90, and $n\in\{20,30\}$, but changes the margins and how disagreement is
distributed across subjects. It retains only the IF-Fisher baseline and the
two most promising boundary hybrids.

```{r extension-setup}
extension_files <- file.path(
  results_dir,
  c(
    "extension_summary.csv", "extension_diagnostics.csv",
    "extension_dgps.csv", "extension_metadata.csv"
  )
)
extension_missing <- extension_files[!file.exists(extension_files)]
if (length(extension_missing) > 0L) {
  stop(paste0(
    "Missing extension results. Run Rscript scripts/run_extension.R ",
    "--reps 750 --bootstrap-reps 199 --cores 1 --progress first."
  ))
}
extension_summary <- read.csv(extension_files[[1L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
extension_diagnostics <- read.csv(extension_files[[2L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
extension_dgps <- read.csv(extension_files[[3L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
extension_metadata_raw <- read.csv(extension_files[[4L]], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
extension_metadata <- setNames(
  extension_metadata_raw$value, extension_metadata_raw$key
)
extension_order <- extension_dgps$dgp
extension_summary <- extension_summary[order(
  match(extension_summary$dgp, extension_order),
  extension_summary$n,
  extension_summary$method
), ]
extension_diagnostics <- extension_diagnostics[order(
  match(extension_diagnostics$dgp, extension_order),
  extension_diagnostics$n
), ]
```

### DGP construction

For the PL rows, let $T\sim\pi$ be the latent true category and set

$$
 \Pr(Y_j=y\mid T=t)
 =p_j\mathbf{1}\{y=t\}+(1-p_j)\pi_y.
$$

With a common $p_j=p$, every rater has margin $\pi$ and quadratic Fleiss kappa
is $p^2$. The uniform and skewed rows therefore both use
$p=\sqrt{0.9}$. For heterogeneous raters,

$$
 \kappa_F=\binom{R}{2}^{-1}\sum_{j<k}p_jp_k,
$$

so the five $p_j$ values are calibrated to make that pair average 0.90.

The rare-failure DGP draws $T\sim\pi$. With probability $1-h$ all raters
report $T$; with probability $h$, an item-wide shock makes every rater draw
independently from $\pi$. Its population coefficient is exactly
$\kappa_F=1-h$, so $h=0.10$.

The local-near-miss DGP uses a transition matrix

$$
 P_e=(1-e)I+eL,
$$

where $L$ moves an interior category left or right with equal probability and
moves an endpoint to its only neighbor. For a generic common transition
matrix $P$, with pooled margin $m=\pi^\mathsf{T}P$,

$$
 A=2\sum_t\pi_t\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid T=t),\qquad
 B=2\operatorname{Var}_{m}(Y),\qquad
 \kappa_F=1-A/B.
$$

The runner solves this finite-state expression for $e$, giving
$e=0.204453$ at $\kappa_F=0.90$. Thus the five DGPs have the same kappa but
very different probabilities that a subject contains any disagreement:

$$
 \Pr(D_i>0)
 =1-\sum_t\pi_t\sum_y P_{ty}^{R}
$$

for the conditionally independent transition rows.

```{r extension-dgp-table}
dgp_tab <- data.frame(
  DGP = extension_dgps$dgp_label,
  Margin = gsub("|", ", ", extension_dgps$margin, fixed = TRUE),
  Tuning = extension_dgps$tuning,
  Kappa = fmt(extension_dgps$true_kappa, 3),
  "Event Probability" = fmt(
    extension_dgps$disagreement_event_probability, 3
  ),
  "Mean Severity Given Event" = fmt(
    extension_dgps$positive_event_severity, 3
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(dgp_tab, align = "llllrr")
```

The last four rows are experiment-defined stress variants of the sourced PL
construction, not claims that one is a universal model for agreement. Their
purpose is to separate low event probability/high severity from high event
probability/low severity while holding the estimand fixed.

### Extension result

```{r extension-answer, results='asis'}
direct <- subset(
  extension_summary, method == "jack_fisher_direct_boundary"
)
boot <- subset(
  extension_summary, method == "bootstrap_t_jack_boundary"
)
if_fisher <- subset(extension_summary, method == "wald_if_fisher")
worst_direct <- direct[which.min(direct$coverage), ]
rare_direct <- subset(direct, dgp == "rare_item_failure" & n == 20)
local_boot <- subset(boot, dgp == "local_near_miss")
cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "The extension confirms that the hybrids are materially better than ",
    "IF-Fisher, but it removes the impression that either is automatically ",
    "calibrated. Across the ten DGP-by-n cells, direct Fisher jackknife-t + ",
    "boundary covers %.3f--%.3f and bootstrap-t + boundary covers %.3f--%.3f; ",
    "their mean absolute deviations from 0.95 are %.3f and %.3f, versus %.3f ",
    "for IF-Fisher. The worst direct cell is **%s, n = %d** at %.3f. ",
    "Rare item-wide failures make the fallback conservative (direct coverage ",
    "%.3f at n = 20), whereas frequent local near-misses need no fallback and ",
    "bootstrap-t covers %.3f/%.3f."
  ),
  min(direct$coverage), max(direct$coverage),
  min(boot$coverage), max(boot$coverage),
  mean(abs(direct$coverage - 0.95)),
  mean(abs(boot$coverage - 0.95)),
  mean(abs(if_fisher$coverage - 0.95)),
  worst_direct$dgp_label, worst_direct$n, worst_direct$coverage,
  rare_direct$coverage,
  local_boot$coverage[local_boot$n == 20],
  local_boot$coverage[local_boot$n == 30]
))
```

```{r extension-coverage-table}
keep <- c("dgp", "dgp_label", "n", "coverage", "mean_length", "fallback_rate")
if_tab <- if_fisher[, keep]
names(if_tab)[4:6] <- c("if_coverage", "if_length", "if_fallback")
direct_tab <- direct[, keep]
names(direct_tab)[4:6] <- c(
  "direct_coverage", "direct_length", "direct_fallback"
)
boot_tab <- boot[, keep]
names(boot_tab)[4:6] <- c(
  "boot_coverage", "boot_length", "boot_fallback"
)
extension_wide <- merge(
  merge(if_tab, direct_tab, by = c("dgp", "dgp_label", "n")),
  boot_tab, by = c("dgp", "dgp_label", "n")
)
extension_wide <- extension_wide[order(
  match(extension_wide$dgp, extension_order), extension_wide$n
), ]
coverage_tab <- data.frame(
  DGP = extension_wide$dgp_label,
  n = extension_wide$n,
  "IF-Fisher Coverage" = fmt(extension_wide$if_coverage, 3),
  "Direct Hybrid Coverage" = fmt(extension_wide$direct_coverage, 3),
  "Bootstrap Hybrid Coverage" = fmt(extension_wide$boot_coverage, 3),
  "Direct Length" = fmt(extension_wide$direct_length, 3),
  "Bootstrap Length" = fmt(extension_wide$boot_length, 3),
  "Direct Fallback" = fmt(extension_wide$direct_fallback, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(coverage_tab, align = "lrrrrrrr")
```

Coverage retains the first-pass convention that an unavailable interval is a
miss. Both boundary hybrids returned an interval in every extension replicate;
IF-Fisher can still be unavailable when the point estimate equals one.

```{r extension-calibration-table}
calibration_rows <- unique(extension_summary[, c(
  "dgp", "dgp_label", "n", "bias", "if_se_ratio", "jackknife_se_ratio"
)])
calibration_rows <- merge(
  calibration_rows,
  extension_diagnostics[, c(
    "dgp", "n", "exact_agreement_rate", "leave_one_out_boundary_rate"
  )],
  by = c("dgp", "n")
)
calibration_rows <- calibration_rows[order(
  match(calibration_rows$dgp, extension_order), calibration_rows$n
), ]
calibration_tab <- data.frame(
  DGP = calibration_rows$dgp_label,
  n = calibration_rows$n,
  Bias = fmt(calibration_rows$bias, 4),
  "IF SE / SD" = fmt(calibration_rows$if_se_ratio, 3),
  "Jackknife SE / SD" = fmt(calibration_rows$jackknife_se_ratio, 3),
  "Exact Agreement" = fmt(calibration_rows$exact_agreement_rate, 3),
  "Leave-One-Out Boundary" = fmt(
    calibration_rows$leave_one_out_boundary_rate, 3
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(calibration_tab, align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Three points survive the extension.

1. **Disagreement geometry matters at fixed kappa.** The event probability is
   about 0.10 for item-wide failures and 0.68 for local near-misses. The former
   frequently triggers the deliberately wide fallback; the latter never does.
2. **The direct hybrid remains attractive, not definitive.** It is simpler
   than nested bootstrap-t and performs well for uniform margins, heterogeneous
   raters, and local near-misses. Coverage of 0.911 for skewed margins at
   $n=30$ rules out a general recommendation from this experiment alone.
3. **The current fallback is too coarse for rare shocks.** Its use of
   $A\leq\Pr(D_i>0)$ discards observed positive-event severity, so 40% fallback
   use at $n=20$ produces conservative coverage and long intervals. A refined
   hurdle or direct ratio-test inversion is the natural next step.

### Reproduce the extension

```sh
Rscript experiments/workbench/48-small-n-jackknife-boundary/scripts/run_extension.R \
  --reps 750 --bootstrap-reps 199 --cores 1 --progress
```

The extension used 750 replications per DGP-by-n cell, 199 outer bootstrap
draws, seed base 484800, and one core. Raw replicate rows remain local-only;
the committed DGP definitions, summaries, diagnostics, and metadata are the
extension record.
